entries.title: Creole tomato
entries.summary: A Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not a single variety: the name comes from the river-soil farms of St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes. Sweet, sharp and juicy, it is a summer crop, eaten raw and cooked into the city's tomato dishes.
entries.guest: Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomatoes, picked ripe on the vine: juicy, sweet and a little sharp. On the tostada they are served raw with heirlooms and burrata.

paras: A Creole tomato is not one variety. It is a tomato grown in Louisiana, left to ripen on the vine and sold close to home. The name belongs first to the growers of St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans on the lower Mississippi, who long sold their fruit as Creole and credited the rich alluvial soil, the silt the river laid down over centuries, for a flavour they said no other tomato had. In the early 1900s tomatoes from the river parishes upstream were simply called Creole too.

Why it matters: a tomato picked ripe tastes of sugar and acid together, sweet, sharp and juicy, with a thin, soft skin. That softness means it bruises easily and will not travel far, so it is a local, seasonal thing, and the kitchen treats it as a visitor from the farm rather than a staple.

LSU muddied the name in 1969, when its researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety actually called Creole. It yielded poorly and the university kept no seed stock of it, so a plant sold as Creole today may not be the original, and the word still means a Louisiana tomato picked ripe, not one cultivar. The season runs from late spring into summer, with the main crop from late May into July, and the city marks it each June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival, a celebration of the tomatoes and the farmers who grow them.

Buy by smell and weight: a ripe Creole tomato smells green and sweet at the stem, feels heavy for its size and gives a little under the thumb. Keep whole ripe tomatoes at room temperature, stem side down and out of the sun, and use them within a day or two. Never chill a whole ripe tomato: below about 10°C (50°F) the flesh turns mealy and the aroma fades. Once it is cut, though, it goes into the cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below, covered and labelled, because the FDA Food Code treats cut tomatoes as a food that needs temperature control.

Raw is where a Creole tomato shines. Slice it thick with a sharp or serrated knife, salt it just before it goes out, and add black pepper and a thread of good oil; salt it too early and the juice runs across the plate. In New Orleans it goes into sandwiches, as the tomato in a po-boy dressed with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise, and into plain tomato salads with onion and herbs.

Cooked, it is the base of Creole sauce, of shrimp Creole and of a Creole courtbouillon, fish stewed in a tomato and roux gravy. To peel a tomato for cooking, cut a shallow cross in the base, drop it into boiling water for 10 to 20 seconds, refresh it in iced water and slip off the skin; peeled, seeded and diced, it becomes concassé. Out of season a good tinned plum tomato, packed ripe, does more for a sauce than a pale winter tomato bought fresh.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada, a dinner starter, Creole tomatoes are mixed with Louisiana heirloom tomatoes and served raw and simply, with creamy burrata on a crisp okra tostada the kitchen makes in house. Smoked tomato water, the clear juice of strained tomatoes with a gentle smoke, is poured around last so the shell stays crisp for the first bites. The dish follows the season and changes when the tomatoes finish. Never name a farm or a parish for tonight's tomatoes unless the kitchen says so at lineup.

Guests often ask whether Creole is a breed of tomato. The honest answer is that the word is older than the 1969 variety and means local and vine-ripened. Sell the tostada as a light first course while the season lasts, and tell the guest to eat it soon after it lands, because the crunch fades within minutes. Any question about what the tostada itself is made with goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: Gulf shrimp
entries.summary: Wild shrimp from the Gulf coast, mostly brown and white, are the backbone of New Orleans cooking. Know the species and their seasons, read the count per pound, cook them briefly and say plainly where they come from.
entries.guest: On the Shrimp & Grits these are wild Louisiana shrimp, from one of the country's great shrimp states: sweet and firm, cooked only until they turn pink.

paras: Gulf shrimp are the wild shrimp caught in the bays, passes and open water of the Gulf coast, and they are the backbone of New Orleans cooking: gumbo, Creole sauce, étouffée (shrimp smothered in a thick sauce over rice), rémoulade (a sharp, spiced cold sauce) and fried shrimp. Louisiana is one of the country's largest shrimp producers, and shrimp is its most valuable commercial fishery.

Three species matter. Brown shrimp come in spring and early summer, in Louisiana's season roughly May to July, and taste a little more of iodine and the sea. White shrimp come in late summer and autumn, roughly mid-August to mid-December, and are sweeter and milder. Pink shrimp, caught mostly off Florida, are mild and sweet and often pinkish even raw. The state opens each area on its biologists' advice.

Shrimp are sold by count: how many make a pound (450 g). U-15 means under 15 to the pound; 16/20 means 16 to 20; 21/25 means 21 to 25. The smaller the number, the larger the shrimp. Words such as jumbo mean different things from one seller to the next, so a cook orders by count; a head-on count differs from a tail count. Look for firm, sweet-smelling shrimp with shells that cling; a smell of ammonia, slime or black spots at the head mean age.

Almost 90 per cent of the shrimp eaten in the United States is imported, much of it farmed in Asia and Latin America. Wild Gulf shrimp taste of the water they lived in and keep the boats and docks of the coast working, which is why a menu that names Louisiana or Gulf shrimp is making a claim worth saying aloud. Louisiana law agrees: since 2019 a restaurant serving imported shrimp or crawfish must say so, on its menu or, where it has none, on a posted sign.

Head-on shrimp keep more flavour, and New Orleans barbecue shrimp is made with them, the fat in the heads enriching the sauce. The heads also spoil first, so head-on shrimp are bought fresh and cooked soon. Save every head and shell for the shrimp stock the Creole kitchen builds its gumbo, étouffée and sauces on: cook them gently in a little oil or butter, stirring, until pink and fragrant, cover with cold water, add onion, celery and bay, simmer gently for 20 to 30 minutes and strain. Longer, and the stock turns bitter and cloudy. To prepare the tails, peel them, run a knife down the back and lift out the dark vein, the gut, which can carry grit.

Shrimp cook in a couple of minutes. Raw, they are grey and translucent; cooked, they turn pink and opaque and curl into a loose C. Pushed further they tighten into an O and turn rubbery: C for cooked, O for overdone. The curl is only a hint, since a split or butterflied shrimp cannot curl; the real test is opaque flesh at the thickest part, and the FDA Food Code's cooking figure for seafood is 63°C (145°F). In a gumbo or a sauce, shrimp go in at the very end.

The fishery is old and many-voiced. By the 1880s the marshes south of New Orleans held villages on stilts around raised platforms where shrimp were dried in the sun for markets in Asia, and at the peak, between 1900 and 1915, there were at least 95 of them. Chinese merchants ran much of the trade, and the shrimpers were Filipino, Chinese, Croatian, Isleño, Cajun, Creole and more.

Shrimp go into the Seafood Gumbo with crab and oysters, top the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits in a Creole sauce with tasso, come as bite-size Popcorn Shrimp with a Crystal gastrique in the Roost, and are fried with French fries on the children's dinner. Use the menu's words: Louisiana shrimp on the Shrimp & Grits and the Popcorn Shrimp, Gulf shrimp on the children's dinner plate. The children's breakfast also has popcorn shrimp with Brabant potatoes; its menu line prints no origin, so say popcorn shrimp and leave the source to the kitchen. Never say all our shrimp are Louisiana, and if a guest asks brown or white, ask the kitchen rather than guess.

On the Shrimp & Grits and the Popcorn Shrimp, where the menu prints Louisiana, a true and easy line: “These are wild Louisiana shrimp, from one of the largest shrimp fisheries in the country.” Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen, never a guess from the floor.

entries.title: Crawfish
entries.summary: Crawfish are small freshwater crustaceans, mostly red swamp crawfish, farmed in Louisiana's rice fields and trapped wild in the Atchafalaya Basin. They are boiled whole in spring, and their tail meat and golden fat carry étouffée, bisque and pies all year.
entries.guest: Crawfish are little freshwater cousins of the lobster and a Louisiana spring tradition. At the Roost they fill the Crawfish Meat Pies, served with a chive rémoulade for dipping.

paras: Crawfish are freshwater crustaceans that look like lobsters no longer than a hand, and in Louisiana they are a season, a party and a pantry staple at once. Say crawfish: crayfish is the textbook word, and crawdad belongs to other parts of the country. Most of what Louisiana sells is the red swamp crawfish, with the white river crawfish a smaller share of the catch.

Louisiana grows nearly all of the country's crawfish. Most are farmed, in ponds and above all in rice fields: crawfish are stocked into the growing rice in late spring and burrow through the summer, and once the rice is harvested and the stubble regrows, the fields are flooded again in autumn, so the same clay soil gives a second crop from late autumn into spring. The rest are trapped wild in the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States.

The season runs roughly January to June and is at its best in spring, when the crawfish are big and both the farms and the basin are producing; wild crawfish usually reach market size in April, May and June. Live crawfish are bought by the sack, lively and smelling of clean water, never of ammonia. The rest of the year the kitchen uses frozen tail meat, peeled and cooked, sold in 450 g (1 lb) packs and often with the fat. It takes 2.7 to 3.2 kg (6 to 7 lb) of live crawfish to give 450 g (1 lb) of tails, a yield of about 15 per cent, which is why peeled tails are dear.

Imported tail meat, much of it from China, is usually cheaper and often washed of most of its fat, and many cooks find it blander and softer. Since 2019 Louisiana law has required a restaurant serving imported crawfish or shrimp to say so, on its menu or, where it has none, on a posted sign, so the label is a question of flavour and of honesty: a guest who asks deserves the kitchen's answer, never a guess.

The boil is the spring ritual. Live crawfish are rinsed in clean water until it runs clear, which washes off mud and grit. As they rinse, pick out and throw away any that are dead: limp and still, or floating. What most people call purging is this rinse: LSU AgCenter research found that emptying the gut takes a 12 to 24 hour soak in fresh water, and that salt in the rinse adds little.

A big pot of water is seasoned fiercely into a court-bouillon, the French kitchen's name for a short, quickly made seasoned cooking liquid (not the Creole fish stew called courtbouillon): salt, cayenne, lemons, onions, garlic and bay, or a ready-made boil, brought to a rolling boil. Potatoes go in first, then corn, then the crawfish, which cook only a few minutes once the pot returns to the boil. Then the heat goes off and they soak for 15 to 30 minutes: the soak, not the boil, is where they drink in the seasoning.

In the kitchen the prize is the tail meat and the fat, the golden paste in the head. It is not fat at all but the hepatopancreas, the organ that does the work of liver and pancreas, and it carries the deep, rich flavour of étouffée, crawfish or shrimp smothered in a thick sauce and served over rice; of bisque, a rich, smooth soup; and of crawfish pie. Good cooks scrape every bit into the pot. It turns quickly, so tails packed with fat are kept cold and used fast.

In the Roost, the Crawfish Meat Pies are the most Louisiana snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list: savoury meat pies filled with crawfish, served with a chive rémoulade for dipping. They follow Louisiana's meat pie tradition, best known from Natchitoches, where a fried half-moon of pastry holds seasoned meat. The menu does not print Louisiana for the crawfish, and the pastry, the filling and the number in an order are not printed either, so each is a question for the kitchen.

Offer the pies to a visitor who wants a local taste with a glass of bubbles. A true line about Louisiana crawfish: most are farmed, many of them in rice fields as a second crop after the rice harvest. A straight tail on a boiled crawfish does not prove it was dead before cooking, whatever a guest has heard. Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Blue crab and lump crabmeat
entries.summary: The blue crab of the Gulf and Atlantic, Louisiana's great crab catch, reaches the kitchen as picked meat sold by grade, as claws and as soft-shells. Know the grades, pick the meat over and fold it gently so the lumps stay whole.
entries.guest: That's Louisiana lump crab: sweet, hand-picked blue crab from the state that catches more of it than any other, warmed gently so it stays tender.

paras: The blue crab, Callinectes sapidus, the beautiful savoury swimmer, lives in the brackish bays and marshes of the Gulf and the Atlantic, where river water meets the sea. It takes its name from the blue of its claws and turns red when cooked. Louisiana runs the largest blue crab fishery in the country and lands about a quarter of the national catch. Most of it is cooked and picked by hand, and the meat reaches kitchens already cooked and chilled, sold by grade, which is why a cook only ever warms crabmeat through, gently, even inside a crab cake or a gratin, and never cooks it hard.

Jumbo lump is the two large muscles that drive the swimming legs, whole, white and costly, kept for dishes where the crab is the show. Lump is large body pieces and broken jumbo, the grade just below jumbo lump. Backfin is smaller flakes of lump with some white body meat. Special is the white flake from the body, good for crab cakes, dips and stuffings. Claw meat is darker, pinkish brown, firmer and sweeter, with a stronger flavour, and it costs least. New Orleans seafood counters often sell just three, jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw, so read each seller's own description of what its backfin lump holds.

Fresh-picked crabmeat keeps only days; pasteurised crabmeat, sealed and heated in its tub, keeps far longer unopened, and the kitchen's labels decide the use-by. Cocktail claws are claws with the shell cracked away and the pincer left on as a handle. They come cooked and are served cold with a sauce for dipping, or warmed in butter; cooked again, the meat tightens onto the cartilage and will not pull free.

Even good crabmeat hides shell and cartilage. To pick it over, spread it in a thin layer on a cold tray and run your fingertips lightly through it, feeling for hard flakes and lifting them out without squeezing the meat; some kitchens use an ultraviolet lamp, under which shell glows. Then treat it gently. Fold lump into a sauce, a stuffing or a filling with a spatula at the very end, lifting from beneath rather than stirring, so the pieces stay whole, and warm it through in butter or sauce. Heated hard, it shreds, dries and loses its sweetness.

A soft-shell crab is a blue crab taken just after it moults, when it has backed out of its old shell and the new one is still soft. Crabbers hold peelers, crabs about to moult, in shedding tanks and lift them out within hours, before the new shell hardens. To clean one, cut away the face behind the eyes, lift the pointed sides of the top shell and pull out the gills, and remove the apron underneath. Then it is fried or sautéed whole and eaten shell and all.

Brennan's prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish, where it crowns the day's fish with a pecan bordelaise, and in the Crab & Corn Omelette with roasted sweet corn and miso butter. Louisiana crab comes with the banana leaf-wrapped Gulf Fish en Papillote, crab joins the shrimp and oysters in the Seafood Gumbo, and the Louisiana Crab Claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette with fines herbes. Say lump, as printed, never jumbo lump, and never name a picking house.

Say aloud that the claws are served warm, so nobody expects a cold cocktail claw, and bring napkins and a plate for the shells: the guest holds the pincer, bites the meat and slides the cartilage out. Whether the claws can come chilled is a question for the chef, and shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Gulf oysters
entries.summary: The eastern oyster of Louisiana's brackish bays: milder and plumper where river water freshens the bay, brinier where the sea pushes in. Eaten raw, chargrilled, fried, baked and in gumbo, and on four Brennan's dishes.
entries.guest: Our Grand Isle Jewels are Louisiana oysters, served raw on the half shell with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette: briny, bright and clean.

paras: Gulf oysters are the eastern oyster, Crassostrea virginica, the species of the Atlantic coast and the Gulf. In Louisiana it grows in brackish water, where the Mississippi and the bayous meet the sea, on natural reefs and on leases: patches of state water bottom that a family rents and tends like a field. Most now come from those private leases, a few from the public reefs and a growing number from cages. From 2003 to 2022 Louisiana accounted for about a third of the country's oyster landings.

Salinity, the saltiness of the water, decides the taste. An oyster takes on the water it filters, so a bed freshened by river water and rain gives a milder, plumper oyster, and a bed near the open Gulf gives a brinier, firmer one. The same bed changes with the weather: milder after a wet spring, saltier after a dry autumn. Warm Gulf water grows oysters fast, and the river keeps many beds fresh, so Gulf oysters are known as large and mild.

Off-bottom farming raises oysters in cages that float or hang above the seabed. Kept off the mud and moved by the tide, they grow cleaner, more even shells, and the farmer can choose saltier water for a brinier oyster. The Grand Isle Jewels grow this way, in floating cages off Grand Isle, a barrier island at the southern edge of Jefferson Parish, where ocean and estuary water mix. Live oysters arrive tightly closed, heavy and smelling of clean sea; a gaping shell that will not close when tapped is dead.

Raw on the half shell, the oyster is shucked to order and sits loose in its liquor, the salty juice in the shell, on crushed ice; the liquor is never poured away. To shuck one, guard the holding hand, pop the hinge with the knife tip, wipe the blade, cut the top muscle, then free the oyster with the cup held level. Cooked, an oyster wants only moments: it is done when its edges, the frilly mantle, begin to curl, and a moment longer shrinks it to a tough button.

Chargrilled oysters go on the half shell over a fierce grill with garlic butter and grated cheese for 3 to 5 minutes, until the butter bubbles and the edges curl. For frying, dredge drained oysters in seasoned cornmeal and fry at 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F) for 1 to 2 minutes, until golden. Baked, they go back into the shell under a topping: Rockefeller's green herb sauce, or Bienville's shrimp, mushroom and creamy white wine sauce. In gumbo they go in at the very end with their liquor; in oyster dressing, the holiday bread stuffing, they are chopped and baked with onion, celery and green pepper.

The old rule says eat oysters only in months with an R in their name, September to April. It began as common sense before refrigeration: oysters spoiled fast in summer heat, and summer is when they spawn, turning soft, watery and milky. Louisiana's public reefs traditionally opened in September; today the state sets each season's dates and areas.

Today the rule has a modern meaning: warm water lets Vibrio, bacteria that live naturally in Gulf water, multiply, and most illness from raw oysters comes in the warm months. Who is most at risk is taught in the raw and cooked oysters entry; every raw oyster question goes to the manager or the kitchen.

Brennan's serves oysters four ways. The Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting, come raw with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette and parsley, briny and bright. The Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch are cooked in New Orleans barbecue sauce, buttery and peppery rather than smoky. Oysters go into the Seafood Gumbo, and smoked oysters into the Creole Caesar's dressing, taking the savoury role anchovy plays. The count per order is a lineup question.

A guest from the East Coast may ask why New Orleans cooks its oysters: Gulf oysters are large and mild, so they take to butter, fire and frying. Steer a guest who wants a briny raw oyster to the Jewels. Tell a guest choosing the Creole Caesar that its dressing is made with smoked oysters; the guide treats it as a shellfish dish, so flag it on the ticket and send shellfish questions to the kitchen. Raw oysters carry the consumer advisory: read the service note and send raw seafood questions to the manager or kitchen.

entries.title: Redfish, drum and the Gulf fish
entries.say: As it reads: redfish, drum, Gulf fish.
entries.summary: Redfish, the red drum, is the Gulf's firm, mild, copper-red fish with a black spot by its tail. Learn it, its cousins and the day's catch, how round and flat fish are cut, and why redfish left commercial nets.
entries.guest: Redfish is the red drum, a firm, mild Gulf fish. Our Gulf fish changes with the day's catch: let me tell you exactly which fish the kitchen has tonight and how it is cooked.

paras: Redfish is the cook's name for the red drum, a fish of the Gulf's bays and shallow coastal water. It is copper red to bronze along the back, paler below, with at least one black spot near the tail. The flesh is white, firm and mild, a little sweet, with a large flake that holds together, so it takes a sear, a sauce or the grill.

Black drum is its larger, coarser cousin: grey to black, with whisker-like barbels under the chin. Smaller black drum eat much like redfish; the very large ones are coarse and seldom kept for the table. The fish on the plate changes with the boats.

Speckled trout, the spotted sea trout, is not a true trout but another drum: soft, delicate and sweet. Flounder is a flat fish with a fine, tender flake. Pompano is small, silver and rich, long prized in the Creole kitchen. Sheepshead, named for its sheep-like teeth, eats crabs and barnacles and has firm, sweet white flesh. Red snapper is firm and sweet under pink skin; grouper is firm with large, moist flakes; tripletail is firm, white and mild. Cobia and amberjack are big, rich, meaty fish, cut into steaks or thick fillets for the grill, with the dark bloodline trimmed away.

A round fish, such as redfish, snapper or trout, has an eye on each side and a backbone down the middle; it gives two fillets. A flat fish, such as flounder, swims on its side with both eyes on top; filleted along the centre line, the classic way, it gives four fillets, two from each side, or it is cooked whole. Skin on, a fillet holds together and can be seared crisp, skin side down, for most of its cooking; skin off, it suits poaching, a papillote (a sealed parcel baked so the fish steams in its own juices) or a crust.

Pin bones are the fine bones in a line down the thicker front half of a round fish fillet. Find them with a fingertip and pull each one with fish tweezers towards the head, the way it lies, so the flesh does not tear.

Fresh fish has clear eyes, red gills, firm flesh that springs back and a clean sea smell; keep it on ice, as near 0°C (32°F) as you can, and use it within a day or two. Cook a fillet until it turns from translucent to opaque and just flakes, 63°C (145°F) at the centre, the figure the USDA gives for fish.

Until the 1980s redfish was an ordinary commercial fish in Louisiana. Around 1980 Paul Prudhomme began serving blackened redfish at K-Paul's in New Orleans and made it famous, and kitchens across the country copied it. The Gulf was fished hard, and the stock fell.

From 1987 federal rules barred a directed commercial redfish fishery in the Gulf's federal waters, and in January 1988 Louisiana banned its commercial harvest too. Red drum is now managed in Louisiana for anglers: state law (R.S. 56:325.3) still prohibits its commercial taking, possession or landing. Redfish on a Louisiana menu today is usually farm raised or comes from outside the state's waters.

Redfish has its own dish at Brennan's: on the Redfish Véronique it stands in for the sole of the French classic, firm enough for a beurre blanc and hibiscus-pickled grapes. Never call it wild Louisiana redfish; where ours comes from is a question for the chef.

The Gulf fish of the day is the day's catch, not one species, on three plates: the Pecan Gulf Fish at breakfast and lunch, the Gulf Fish en Papillote at dinner and the children's sautéed Gulf fish with potato and green beans. Never call the Véronique's redfish the Gulf fish of the day: it is its own fish, with its own story.

Every table asks what the fish is tonight, so learn it at lineup, never guess, and give it with its texture: flaky and delicate, or firm and meaty. If the kitchen has not said, offer to ask. A guest who remembers blackened redfish will enjoy the story of why it left the commercial nets. Questions about bones or allergies are answered from the service note and the kitchen, never from memory.

entries.title: Andouille
entries.summary: Cajun andouille is a coarse pork sausage, heavy with garlic and pepper and smoked for hours until dark and firm. It is made to season a pot, browned first so its fat and smoke flavour gumbo, jambalaya and red beans.
entries.guest: Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, is Louisiana's coarse, smoked pork sausage, firm and smoky rather than juicy. In our Seafood Gumbo it gives a smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters.

paras: Andouille is south Louisiana's smoked seasoning sausage: pork shoulder and its fat, cut coarse, seasoned hard with garlic, black pepper and cayenne, stuffed into a wide casing and smoked low for hours until it is dark brown and firm. Cut one open and you see big, distinct pieces of meat rather than a fine paste.

It is not a sausage for the grill plate. Firm and smoky rather than juicy, it is made to season a pot, and a little of it carries smoke, salt, fat and heat through a whole gumbo. In Creole and Cajun cooking it works as much as a seasoning as the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper.

Pork shoulder, which runs roughly three parts lean to one of fat, is cut into large dice or ground through a coarse plate, about 10 mm. Season it with salt at 1.75 to 2 per cent of the meat's weight, plenty of fresh garlic, coarse black pepper and cayenne, often a little thyme, and pink curing salt no. 1 (salt with sodium nitrite) at the dose its maker prints. The cure keeps the meat pink and guards against the bacteria that like the low, slow heat of a smokehouse.

Curing salt is weighed to the gram, never guessed, and kept apart from table salt: making andouille is charcutier's work, the craft of the pork butcher and sausage maker, done under a senior cook, while a Commis masters the browning and the timing in the pot.

Mix the seasoned meat until it turns tacky, stuff it firmly and tie it in links. Let the links dry until the surface is tacky, then smoke them low, starting around 60°C (140°F) to dry them and take the smoke, and raise the heat to 75 to 80°C (167 to 176°F) over several hours, traditionally over pecan wood in LaPlace, until the centre reaches 71°C (160°F), the USDA mark for cooked ground pork.

In the pot, cut andouille into half-moons about 1 cm (about ½ inch) thick and brown them in a heavy pot over medium heat for 5 to 8 minutes, until the edges colour and the fat runs. Lift them out: the smoky fat now flavours the roux or the trinity. In a brown jambalaya the browned bits on the bottom of the pot colour the rice; in red beans the andouille simmers for hours with the beans. Return it to simmer so its smoke spreads through the liquid.

French andouille is a different thing. Andouille de Vire from Normandy and andouille de Guémené from Brittany are made from the pig's chitterlings, its intestines and stomach, smoked and cooked, then sliced cold; the Guémené shows neat rings when cut. Andouillette is the smaller cousin, chitterlings and often tripe, grilled hot and served with mustard, with a strong, farmyard smell. Louisiana kept the name and the smoke and filled the casing with shoulder meat instead, so warn a guest who expects the French one before they order.

Louisiana andouille is a River Parishes sausage. The German farmers of the German Coast, upriver from New Orleans, brought a strong tradition of sausage making, with French, Acadian and other influences beside it. The town that made it famous is LaPlace, in St. John the Baptist Parish, which calls itself the Andouille Capital of the World: Governor Edwin Edwards proclaimed the title in the 1970s, and the first Andouille Festival was held there in October 1972; today the parish runs it each October. LaPlace andouille is known for its pecan wood smoke.

Unbrowned andouille dropped into a finished pot stays rubbery and gives little; browned first, it gives its fat and smoke to everything after it. Scorched edges taste bitter, so keep the heat at medium. Andouille brings its own salt and pepper, so a gumbo salted before the sausage has simmered is easily oversalted: season at the end.

At Brennan's andouille is in the Seafood Gumbo, the smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters, served over popcorn rice. The menu names no maker: never say ours is from LaPlace or from a named smokehouse unless the kitchen confirms it.

Say ahn-DOO-ee. Describe it as a coarse, smoked pork sausage, firm and smoky, that seasons the gumbo. Andouille is pork, so tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order. Questions about anything else in the bowl go to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Tasso
entries.say: TAH-so (TASS-oh is also heard; confirm the house habit)
entries.summary: Tasso is Cajun seasoning meat: strips of pork shoulder briefly cured, coated in cayenne, garlic and spice, and hot-smoked until firm. Diced small, a little seasons a whole pot of beans, gumbo or Creole sauce.
entries.guest: Tasso, TAH-so, is Cajun smoked pork shoulder, spiced with cayenne and garlic. It seasons our Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits, so the sauce is smoky as well as tangy.

paras: Tasso is south Louisiana's seasoning meat. Cooks cut strips of pork shoulder, cure them briefly in salt and sugar, coat them thickly in cayenne, garlic and other spices, and hot-smoke them until firm and cooked through. It is sometimes called Cajun ham, but the name misleads: it comes from the shoulder, not the hind leg, and it is far too spicy and smoky to slice and eat like ham.

A little does a great deal: diced and cooked into a dish, tasso spreads smoke, salt and heat through the whole pot. It is tied by tradition to the boucherie, the communal hog killing of Acadiana, where neighbours shared every part of the pig and lean trimmings became seasoning meat.

Cut pork shoulder (the butt) across the grain into strips about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick, trimming the heaviest fat. Cure them in salt and sugar with pink curing salt no. 1 at the dose its maker prints. The boucherie's cure is brief, three or four hours; many modern makers dry-cure the strips in the fridge for a day or two, measuring salt at 2 to 2.5 per cent of the meat's weight. Rinse, pat dry and coat every side thickly with the rub: cayenne, paprika, black and white pepper and garlic, often with thyme, marjoram or allspice.

Leave the strips uncovered in the fridge until the surface is dry and tacky, a few hours or overnight, so the smoke clings. Hot-smoke them over pecan, hickory or oak at about 95 to 110°C (203 to 230°F) for 2 to 4 hours, until the centre reaches at least 63°C (145°F), the USDA mark for whole cuts of pork; many smokehouses take it to around 68°C (155°F) for a firmer piece. Cool, wrap and keep it chilled; it freezes well in small portions.

Tasso is used by the spoonful, not the slice. Dice it small, about 5 mm (¼ inch), and render it gently, cooking it slowly so its fat melts out, in a little butter or oil over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes before the trinity goes in, so the spices bloom without scorching. As a rough measure, 115 g (4 oz) of diced tasso seasons about 1 litre (about 1 quart) of Creole sauce, beans or gumbo. For a cream sauce for pasta, the cream is reduced over the browned tasso until it coats a spoon. Season every dish only at the end: tasso brings its own salt.

Country ham is a different thing from the same pig: the hind leg, dry-cured in salt for weeks and aged for months, often smoked, and eaten in thin slices or fried; it is salty and deep rather than hot. Tasso is the shoulder, cured for hours or days, hot-smoked until cooked and coated in pepper, a seasoning rather than a slice. Andouille is a sausage, coarse chopped meat and fat in a casing, garlicky where tasso is lean and fiery, though both are browned to season a pot.

Tasso fails in the pan more often than in the smokehouse. Thick pieces give a mouthful of salt and cayenne; the pepper crust scorches at high heat and turns bitter; added cold at the end, it never gives its smoke to the liquid.

At Brennan's tasso seasons the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, a breakfast and lunch entrée: Louisiana shrimp in a tomato sauce built on the holy trinity, over a fried pimento cheese grit cake with fried okra chips. The tasso makes the sauce smoky as well as tangy. The menu names no maker, so ask the kitchen before saying it is smoked in-house or bought from a named smokehouse.

Both TAH-so and TASS-oh are heard in Louisiana; the house guide writes TAH-so, so confirm the house habit and follow it. If a guest calls it Cajun ham, explain that it is shoulder, not leg, a seasoning meat. Tasso is pork, so flag it for a guest who avoids pork before they order the Shrimp & Grits, and tell them the house guide rates the dish mild to moderate in spice.

entries.title: Boudin
entries.summary: Cajun boudin is a fresh sausage of cooked pork, pork liver, rice, onion, green onion and pepper, heated in its casing and eaten hot, squeezed from the skin. It is Acadiana's everyday snack, sold by the link at meat markets and roadside counters.
entries.guest: Boudin, BOO-dan, is Acadiana's pork and rice sausage, soft and peppery, eaten hot and squeezed from its casing. It is a roadside food of Cajun country rather than one of our dishes.

paras: Boudin is the sausage of Acadiana, the Cajun parishes of south-west Louisiana. Cajun boudin blanc, white boudin, is pork shoulder and pork liver, simmered tender, minced and mixed with cooked rice, onion, green onion, parsley, bell pepper, black pepper and cayenne, then stuffed into a casing. Everything is cooked before it goes in, so the link is only heated through. It eats soft, moist and peppery, closer to a rice dressing in a casing than to a firm sausage, and the filling is squeezed hot from the skin.

It is a lesson in thrift from the boucherie, the communal pig killing where neighbours shared every part: boudin uses the liver, the trimmings and the rich cooking broth, and stretches them with rice from the fields nearby.

Simmer pork shoulder in large pieces with onion, celery, bell pepper and seasoning, in water just to cover, for 1.5 to 2 hours, until it falls apart. Add the pork liver, roughly one part to three or four of shoulder, for the last 30 minutes, so it cooks through without turning grainy. Lift everything out, keep the broth, and grind the meat, liver and vegetables through a coarse plate, about 6 mm (1/4 inch).

Fold the meat into hot cooked long-grain rice with plenty of green onion and parsley, then loosen it with broth until moist and spoonable: the broth carries the flavour and keeps the rice from drying in the casing. Roughly equal weights of meat and rice is a common start. Season it hard while hot, then stuff it loosely into hog casings and twist it into links.

To serve, heat the links in water held at 80 to 85°C (176 to 185°F), well below the boil, for 10 to 15 minutes, or steam them; boiling bursts the casing. Boudin made ahead and reheated for hot holding should reach 74°C (165°F) in the centre and then be kept at 57°C (135°F) or above, as the FDA Food Code sets out.

Boudin rouge, red boudin, adds pig's blood to the same pork and rice, turning it dark and rich. It belongs to the boucherie and the home kitchen and is now rare in commerce, so most guests know only the white one. Boudin balls are the filling without the casing: chilled until firm, rolled into balls about 4 cm (1.5 inches) across, dipped in seasoned flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, and fried at 175°C (347°F) for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden.

France's boudins are distant cousins that share the name and little else. French boudin blanc is a fine, pale sausage of pork, chicken or veal bound with milk or cream and egg, poached, then browned in butter. Boudin noir is the French blood sausage, pig's blood, fat and slow-cooked onion, poached and seared crisp, classic with apples. Neither carries rice, which is what makes the Cajun one Cajun.

Boudin is sold hot from steamers at meat markets, grocery counters and petrol stations across Acadiana, by the link or by the pound, often for breakfast. Visitor guides map a boudin trail of these counters through the parishes around Lafayette, and towns compete for the title: in 2012 the Louisiana Legislature named Scott, just west of Lafayette, the Boudin Capital of the World. How the Acadians came to the prairies is told in the Creole and Cajun entry.

Dry, crumbly boudin had too little broth or too much rice: loosen the filling before stuffing. Burst links were boiled or stuffed too tight. A pasty filling came from overcooked rice or hard mixing, so cook the rice just tender and fold, never beat. Bland boudin was seasoned cold; rice dulls salt and pepper, so taste the hot filling and season it hard.

Say BOO-dan. Brennan's menus print no boudin, so a guest who asks is asking about Louisiana, not the menu: describe it as Acadiana's pork and rice sausage, eaten hot from its casing, then offer the Cajun meats the house does serve, andouille in the Seafood Gumbo and tasso in the Creole sauce of the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Questions about what goes into any dish go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Filé
entries.summary: Filé is the ground dried leaf of the sassafras tree, a Choctaw ingredient taken up by Creole and Cajun cooks. Earthy and woody, with a hint of root beer, it seasons and thickens gumbo, and it goes in off the heat.
entries.guest: Filé, FEE-lay, is ground sassafras leaves, earthy and a little like root beer. It came to Louisiana cooking from the Choctaw, and it thickens a gumbo.

paras: Filé is a fine, olive-green powder made from the dried leaves of the sassafras tree, which grows wild across the eastern United States. It is a Choctaw ingredient, taken up by Creole and Cajun cooks; the Creole roots entry tells how. In a Louisiana kitchen it does two jobs at once: it seasons, with a smell all its own, and it thickens, giving a gumbo body and a faint silkiness.

Its taste and smell are earthy and woody, a little like eucalyptus, with a hint of root beer, which is no accident: root beer was traditionally flavoured with sassafras root. Fresh filé smells green and lively the moment the jar opens. A gumbo thickened with it, rather than with okra, is called a gumbo filé.

Making filé is simple and slow. Sassafras leaves are picked, dried in the shade until brittle, then pounded or ground and sifted to a fine powder, with the stems and coarse veins sieved out so it is not gritty.

In a gumbo, filé goes in at the end, off the heat, or as a pinch over the bowl at the table; boiled, it turns stringy. The gumbo thickeners entry teaches how filé, okra and roux share the work, with the doses and the faults.

Buy filé in small jars and read the label. Pure filé lists only ground sassafras leaves; some blends are cut with thyme or other herbs, which change the taste and weaken the thickening, so a cook who wants control buys it pure. Look for a fresh olive-green colour and a strong green, woody smell; brown, dusty powder that smells of hay has lost its aroma. Filé fades fast once opened. Keep it sealed, in a cool, dark cupboard away from the stove, and use it within a few months.

Most of filé's faults happen in the gumbo pot, and the gumbo thickeners entry teaches them. In the jar the fault is age: a flat, dusty taste and weak thickening mean old filé, or a blend cut with other herbs, so smell the jar before it goes near the pot.

Sassafras root and bark carry safrole, the main part of sassafras oil, which the US Food and Drug Administration barred as a food additive in 1960; that is why root beer is now flavoured without it. Safrole sits mostly in the root and bark rather than in the leaves that filé is made from. Even so, a guest's health question about filé, as about any ingredient, goes to the kitchen; a server never answers it from the floor.

Brennan's menus do not list filé. The house's published Seafood Gumbo recipe carries filé, with okra and tomato, but the menu lists none of them, so whether tonight's gumbo has filé is a question for the kitchen, confirmed at lineup and never promised from the published recipe.

Say FEE-lay. Describe filé as ground sassafras leaves, earthy and woody with a hint of root beer, which came to Louisiana cooking from the Choctaw and thickens a gumbo. A guest who asks for filé is asking for the old custom of a pinch over the bowl: ask the kitchen whether there is any to send.

entries.title: Okra
entries.summary: Okra is the green seed pod of a plant in the mallow family, carried from West and Central Africa through the slave trade. Cut and simmered, it releases a slippery gel that thickens gumbo; fried or pickled, it stays crisp.
entries.guest: Okra, OH-kruh, is the pod from West and Central Africa that gave gumbo its name. Ours is crisp: the dinner tostada under the Creole tomatoes, and fried chips on the daytime Shrimp & Grits.

paras: Okra is the seed pod of a tall, heat-loving plant of the mallow family, kin to cotton and hibiscus. The pods are ridged, green and finger-length, filled with soft white seeds. Okra came to the Americas from West and Central Africa through the slave trade, with the enslaved cooks who knew how to use it, and the word gumbo most likely comes from ki ngombo, a word for okra in the Bantu languages of west-central Africa. The Creole roots entry tells that story.

What makes okra matter in the kitchen is its mucilage, the clear, slippery gel that seeps from a cut pod as it heats in liquid. In a gumbo or a stew it thickens, giving body and a silky feel; in the wrong dish it reads as slime. Every okra method is a choice about the mucilage: cook it down long in fat to tame it, use it to thicken, or cook the pods fast and dry so it never shows.

To tame it, smother the okra: cut it in rounds and cook it slowly in fat with onion, often with tomato, stirring now and then, for 45 minutes to an hour, until the ropy strings cook away and it turns soft and silky. Acid helps, which is why okra and tomato are old partners. To avoid it, keep the pods whole or cut them only just before cooking, keep them dry, and use high, dry heat: frying, roasting or a hot grill.

For fried okra, slice pods into rounds about 1 cm (about 1/2 inch) thick, toss them in buttermilk, then in seasoned cornmeal, and fry at 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F) for 3 to 4 minutes until golden; drain on a rack and salt at once. Okra and tomatoes is stewed with onion, often with bacon or shrimp. Pickled okra is whole pods packed in a hot vinegar brine with garlic, chilli and dill, crisp and never slippery.

Choose small, firm, bright green pods about 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) long that snap cleanly at the tip. Pods much past 10 cm (4 inches) turn woody and stringy and stay tough however long they cook. Avoid dark patches and soft ends. Okra bruises and blackens quickly: keep it dry and unwashed in a paper bag in the fridge, use it within two or three days, and wash and dry it just before cutting. In Louisiana it is a summer crop; frozen cut okra serves the rest of the year.

Slimy okra in a dish meant to be crisp was wet, crowded or cut too early: dry the pods, cut them just before cooking and fry in small batches so the oil stays hot. Tough, fibrous pieces came from overgrown pods. Greasy fried okra met oil that was too cool. Okra that darkens in the pot has usually met copper, brass or bare iron, or simply cooked too long. The darkening is harmless, and a well-seasoned black iron pot, the traditional gumbo pot, is fine for a dark gumbo; use stainless steel or enamel when the okra must stay green.

At Brennan's okra is served crisp. On the Creole Tomato Tostada the tostada itself, a flat, crisp shell, is housemade with okra, and the smoked tomato water goes on last so the shell stays crunchy for the first bites. On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, fried okra chips go on top for crunch. The Brennan's Bloody Mary carries pickled okra and spicy beans standing in the glass. The house's published gumbo recipe carries okra, but the menu does not list it in the Seafood Gumbo, so never promise it there; whether tonight's gumbo has it is confirmed at lineup.

Say OH-kruh. A guest who fears slime can be told that ours is crisp, never slippery, and that the tostada is best eaten soon after it lands, as the crunch fades within minutes. The menu does not say whether the okra tostada is made on masa or wheat, so a gluten question goes to the kitchen, as does any question about the coating or the fryer for the okra chips.

entries.title: Louisiana rice
entries.summary: Louisiana grows its rice on the south-west prairie around Crowley, and rice sits under or inside most Creole and Cajun dishes. Long grain is the everyday rice, cooked to stay separate; popcorn rice is the aromatic local long grain.
entries.guest: Our Seafood Gumbo sits on Louisiana popcorn rice, an aromatic long grain that really does smell a little of popcorn as it cooks.

paras: Rice is the starch of Creole and Cajun cooking. Gumbo, étouffée and red beans are served over it; jambalaya and rice dressing are cooked with it. Louisiana grows its own on the prairie of south-west Louisiana, in the parishes around Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish, which calls itself the Rice Capital of America and first held its rice festival, now the International Rice Festival, in 1937.

Long grain is the everyday rice: slender grains that cook up dry and separate, so they sit under a gumbo without turning to paste. Louisiana also grows medium grain, softer and stickier. Popcorn rice is the local speciality, an aromatic long grain of the Della type developed in Louisiana, which smells of popcorn as it cooks. The aroma comes from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the molecule that also scents basmati, jasmine and fresh popcorn; there is no popcorn in the bag.

For rice that stays separate under a gumbo or étouffée, rinse it in cold water, swirling and draining two or three times until the water runs nearly clear; that washes off loose surface starch, the glue of gummy rice. Measure the water: for rinsed long grain, about 1.5 parts water to 1 part rice by volume, so 1 cup (240 ml) of rice to 1.5 cups (360 ml) of water, with salt and a little butter. Aromatic rice may want a little less; follow the bag.

Bring it to the boil, stir once, cover tightly and turn the heat to its lowest for 15 to 18 minutes, without lifting the lid. Take it off the heat and rest it, still covered, for 10 minutes, so the steam finishes the grains evenly, then fluff it with a fork. The old Creole way, still used for large batches, boils rice in plenty of salted water like pasta, drains it and lets it steam dry, covered, over the lowest heat or in a low oven. Either way, the rice goes into the bowl first and the gumbo over it: rice never cooks in the gumbo pot.

Rice dressing and dirty rice turn rice into a meal. Brown ground pork or beef, add chicken livers and gizzards, the gizzards simmered tender first and both chopped fine, then the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, with garlic, a little stock and sometimes a spoonful of roux, and simmer until thick. Fold in cold cooked rice, about equal weights of rice and meat, with green onion and parsley. Dirty rice is usually said to take its name from the colour browned livers give it, though cooks disagree over which of the two dishes carries the livers. Jambalaya and red beans have their own entries.

Rice growing on the south-west prairie began in earnest in the early 1880s, and the Rice Research Station at Crowley, opened in 1909 and now run by the LSU AgCenter, has bred Louisiana rice for more than a century. The fields do double duty: after the rice harvest many farmers flood them again and raise crawfish in the stubble from winter into spring, a rotation the crawfish entry explains.

Cooked rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus, a bacterium that survives cooking and grows if the rice sits warm. Hold rice hot at 57°C (135°F) or above, or cool it fast and shallow: from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within two hours, and to 5°C (41°F) within six hours in all, as the FDA Food Code sets out. Cold cooked rice is exactly what rice dressing wants, so cool it right the day before.

At Brennan's the Seafood Gumbo is served over Louisiana popcorn rice. If a guest notices a nutty, toasty smell as the bowl lands, that is the rice, not the roux, and a nice detail to share; the roux, which the published recipe takes to a dark mahogany, gives the gumbo its colour and depth. The menu names no mill, so never name one. The South Louisiana Rice Dressing is a dinner side with no printed description: confirm the meats at lineup, pork, beef or chicken liver, before describing it, and never offer it as a vegetable side.

Describe the rice dressing as south Louisiana's stuffing: rice folded into browned, seasoned meat and the trinity, a cousin of dirty rice and a Sunday and holiday dish. Meat and dietary questions about it go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Cane syrup and Steen's
entries.say: As it reads: cane syrup and Steen's.
entries.summary: Pure cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles to a dark, glossy syrup with nothing taken out. Gentler than molasses and different from sorghum, it is Louisiana's pouring syrup, and Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910.
entries.guest: The peaches are glazed in Louisiana cane syrup: cane juice simply boiled down, lighter and more buttery than molasses, sweet and caramelised against the rich duck.

paras: Cane syrup is the juice of sugar cane boiled down until it is thick, dark and glossy, with nothing taken out and, in the traditional style, nothing added. It tastes of caramel and toffee with a soft, buttery depth, gentler and rounder than molasses. Louisiana pours it the way New England pours maple syrup: over biscuits and pain perdu, the city's French toast, into cakes and pies, and onto meat and fruit as a glaze. For a cook it is a sweetener that brings colour and flavour at once; for a server it is a story of Louisiana's sugar country.

The cane is cut in autumn and crushed between heavy rollers to press out a grey-green juice that is mostly water, only around a sixth of it sugar. The juice is strained, then boiled in wide, open kettles. As it heats, a scum of plant matter rises and is skimmed off again and again, which keeps the syrup clear and clean tasting.

Hours of boiling drive off the water and darken the syrup as its sugars brown. The cook stops at a set thickness, judged by a thermometer reading well above water's boiling point, usually around 106 to 108°C (223 to 226°F), a hydrometer or the way the syrup sheets from a paddle. Several litres of juice make one litre of syrup.

Treat it as a sugar that brings its own flavour. It browns and then burns faster than white sugar, so brush it on in the last minutes of cooking: peach halves roasted at 200°C (392°F) for 10 to 15 minutes take their brush of cane syrup and a little melted butter for the last 5 minutes. For a quick gastrique, the French sweet and sour reduction that classically starts from caramelised sugar, simmer equal parts cane syrup and vinegar until reduced by about half and the syrup coats a spoon. It takes the place of corn syrup in a Louisiana pecan pie, sweetens barbecue sauces and bakes into gâteau de sirop, the Cajun syrup cake.

Molasses is a by-product of making sugar. Cane juice is boiled until sugar crystals form, the crystals are spun out, and the dark syrup left behind is molasses; each further boiling takes out more sugar and leaves a darker, more bitter molasses, the last and strongest called blackstrap. Cane syrup keeps all its sugar, so it is sweeter, milder and lighter. Sorghum syrup is the juice of sweet sorghum, a tall grass rather than sugar cane, boiled down the same way: thinner and tangier, with an earthy, slightly sour edge, and more at home in the Upper South. Golden syrup, the British tin, is a pale refinery syrup, mild beside all three.

Sugar made south Louisiana. In the 1790s planters learned to granulate Louisiana cane into sugar at a profit, and plantations spread along the river, a wealth built on the forced labour of enslaved people. Cane still grows across a crescent of parishes from the river above New Orleans west to Bayou Teche, and the harvest, called grinding, runs from early autumn into midwinter. Steen's began in 1910, when an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane near Abbeville and, rather than lose it, he milled it into syrup. The family still runs the mill on Bayou Vermilion and cooks in open kettles, adding nothing, which is why the yellow tin reads 100% Pure Cane Syrup.

On the dinner tasting, cane syrup glazes the peaches of the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast: sweet, caramelised fruit against rich duck, with candied hazelnuts for crunch. The menu says cane syrup and names no maker, so call it Louisiana cane syrup and never say Steen's is on the plate unless the kitchen confirms it. The duck course has appeared in two versions on the house's own pages, so describe the one printed tonight and confirm it at lineup.

Guests often ask whether it is molasses. Say no: molasses is what is left once sugar has been taken out, while cane syrup is the whole juice simply boiled down, lighter, sweeter and more buttery. A curious guest may enjoy the Steen's story, a 1910 freeze turned into a Louisiana staple, told as the story of the style rather than of the kitchen's bottle.

entries.title: Creole mustard
entries.summary: A coarse, spicy whole-grain mustard of brown mustard seeds steeped in vinegar, often sharpened with horseradish. New Orleans keeps it for rémoulade, sandwiches, glazes, crab cakes and dressings, and its heat is fragile: it fades with boiling.
entries.guest: Creole mustard is New Orleans' own grainy, spicy mustard: brown seeds steeped in vinegar, often sharpened with horseradish, so it is coarser and tangier than Dijon.

paras: Creole mustard is a coarse, grainy mustard made from brown mustard seeds soaked in vinegar, then partly ground so that some seeds stay whole. Many versions add horseradish, salt and spices. It is coarser and more vinegary than Dijon, often with a horseradish kick, and nothing like the mild yellow mustard of the ballpark, with a tangy, nose-tingling heat and a pop of whole seed. In New Orleans it is the pantry mustard: it builds the pink Creole rémoulade, spreads on ham and roast beef sandwiches, binds crab cakes and sharpens glazes and vinaigrettes, the oil and vinegar dressings.

Mustard's heat is made, not stored. A dry seed is mild. Crack it and wet it, and an enzyme in the seed turns a sulphur compound into a sharp, volatile oil, the same family of heat as horseradish and wasabi, which rises into the nose rather than burning the tongue. Brown seeds make plenty of it; the yellow seeds of American mustard make a milder, gentler heat. Acid slows the enzyme, so a mustard made with vinegar is steadier and gentler than powder mixed with cold water, and heat stops it altogether and drives the oil away.

That chemistry decides when the mustard goes in. Stir Creole mustard into a hot sauce or pan juices off the heat, at the very end, and do not let it boil again: boiling drives off the heat and can leave the mustard bitter and grainy. In a glaze for the oven, expect the bite to soften into a tangy warmth, and brush on a little fresh mustard as the meat comes out if you want the heat back. In a vinaigrette, the fine particles and gum of the ground seed coat cling round the oil droplets and slow the oil and vinegar from parting.

To make a Creole-style mustard, soak 100 g (3.5 oz) of brown mustard seeds in 120 ml (4 fl oz) of white or cider vinegar and 60 ml (2 fl oz) of water for 24 to 48 hours at room temperature, adding a little more liquid if the seeds drink it all. Blend half the seeds to a coarse paste with 5 g of salt and a spoonful of grated horseradish, stir in the rest whole and refrigerate. It tastes harsh and bitter at first and mellows over 3 to 5 days.

Dijon is smooth: brown or black seeds with the hulls sieved out, traditionally mixed with white wine or verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes, for a clean, sharp heat. Moutarde à l'ancienne, old-style French whole-grain mustard, is Creole mustard's nearest European cousin but is usually milder and winier. American yellow mustard is made from the milder yellow seed, coloured with turmeric and thinned with vinegar: bright, mild and smooth. Creole mustard sits at the coarse, vinegary end of the shelf, its heat set by the brand and the horseradish.

The brand most New Orleans cooks know is Zatarain's, a New Orleans brand founded in 1889 and now owned by McCormick, which grew from root beer extract into seasonings, pickles and mustards; its Creole mustard is stone ground. Where the style began is not documented. A story often told on labels and in food writing credits the German families who farmed the German Coast, the river parishes upriver from New Orleans settled in the French colonial years, with bringing a coarse mustard tradition from home. We have found no record that confirms it, so tell it as a story, not as fact.

A guest who knows Dijon may expect something smooth and mild; tell them Creole mustard is coarser and tangier, with whole seeds that pop. Where a guest asks which mustard is in a dish, or whether a dish carries mustard at all, the kitchen has the answer: never guess a brand or a recipe. Mustard is a listed allergen in some countries, and every allergen question goes to the kitchen.

entries.say: As it reads: Louisiana hot sauces.
entries.summary: Louisiana-style hot sauce is aged red peppers, vinegar and salt, thin enough to shake. Tabasco from Avery Island and Crystal from New Orleans are the two famous bottles, and the table uses them to season, not to burn.
entries.guest: The Popcorn Shrimp comes with a gastrique made with Crystal, New Orleans' own hot sauce since 1923: sweet, tangy and gently spicy, for dipping.

paras: A Louisiana-style hot sauce is three things: ripe red peppers, salt and vinegar. The peppers are mashed with salt and aged, then thinned with vinegar and strained into a thin red sauce that shakes from the bottle. The vinegar and the ageing matter as much as the heat: a Louisiana sauce tastes bright and tangy first and hot second. That is why New Orleans treats it as a seasoning, shaken on at the table the way you would squeeze a lemon, rather than as a test of nerve.

Tabasco is made by the McIlhenny family on Avery Island, a salt dome rising from the marsh near New Iberia, and has been since 1868. Tabasco peppers are picked by hand when fully red and mashed with salt, and the mash is packed into white oak barrels under a cap of salt to age for up to three years. It is then mixed with distilled vinegar, stirred for weeks and strained. The result is thin, sharp and fiercely tangy, with a quick, clean heat.

Crystal is the New Orleans bottle. In 1923 Alvin Baumer bought a small company on Tchoupitoulas Street making syrup for snowballs, the city's shaved ice, and it came with a recipe for a pepper sauce; Baumer Foods, still family owned, has made Crystal ever since, today upriver in Reserve. It is aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt: milder than Tabasco and more vinegar-forward, so it reads tangy before hot. It is the bottle on tables across the city.

In the kitchen, hot sauce goes in late. Long boiling flattens the vinegar's brightness, so add it at the end or leave it for the guest. It also builds a gastrique, a French sweet and sour reduction: cook about 100 g (3.5 oz) of sugar to a light caramel, loosen it carefully with 120 ml (4 fl oz) of vinegar and hot sauce together, then reduce until the syrup coats a spoon. The sugar rounds off the heat and the vinegar cuts through fried or rich food.

Creole seasoning is a different tool. It is a dry blend built on paprika, cayenne and black pepper, with garlic and onion powder, dried thyme and oregano, and usually salt. Hot sauce brings acid, liquid and heat; the dry blend brings colour, warmth and savour, and it clings to meat and fish before they cook. Because most blends carry salt, season with the blend first and add salt only after tasting. Think of hot sauce as a finish and Creole seasoning as a rub or a base.

On the Bubbles at Brennan's list in the Roost Bar, the Popcorn Shrimp comes with a Crystal gastrique for dipping: sweet, tangy and gently spicy against crisp fried Louisiana shrimp. How sweet or hot tonight's batch runs is a question for the kitchen. The house also makes its own Creole spice, printed on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak. The blend is not printed, so describe it as warm and savoury rather than fiery and send any question about a particular spice to the kitchen.

At the table, New Orleans shakes hot sauce onto raw oysters with lemon and horseradish, into gumbo, over red beans and rice and onto eggs. When a guest asks for hot sauce, bring what the house stocks and name it; never promise a brand you have not seen on hand. Describe Crystal as tangy before hot and Tabasco as sharper and hotter. A guest who finds a dish too hot will get more relief from butter or a creamy side than from water, because the heat of chilli dissolves in fat, not water; bread helps too, by soaking it up.

entries.title: Chicory coffee
entries.summary: Roasted, ground chicory root blended with coffee: a darker, more bitter, fuller cup with less caffeine than straight coffee. A French habit New Orleans kept, poured as café au lait at the French Market and baked into Brennan's Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
entries.guest: Chicory is a roasted root blended into our New Orleans coffee, a French habit the city kept; it gives a roasty, chocolatey depth, and it is baked into the coffee cake.

paras: Chicory coffee is ordinary coffee blended with the roasted, ground root of the chicory plant. The root has no coffee in it and carries no caffeine of its own; roasted, it turns dark and bittersweet, with a roasty, slightly chocolatey taste. Blended with coffee it makes a darker, more bitter cup with a smooth, full body, and because part of every spoonful is root rather than bean, a cup carries less caffeine than the same cup of straight coffee. In New Orleans it is the taste of the morning, strong and dark and often softened with hot milk.

The root is dug, washed, cut into small pieces, dried and roasted, much as coffee beans are, until it is deep brown, then ground and blended with ground coffee, usually a dark roast. Blends run from a little chicory to a good deal, and the proportion is the roaster's choice. Chicory gives up its colour and body faster than coffee, so a blend brews strong: use a little less than you would of straight coffee, about 50 g (1.75 oz) to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of water, just off the boil at 90 to 96°C (194 to 205°F).

Café au lait, coffee with milk, is made the New Orleans way with equal parts strong chicory coffee and hot milk, the milk heated until it steams, about 65°C (149°F), and never boiled, which gives it a skin and a cooked taste. Its home is the French Market, where Café du Monde has poured café au lait with chicory since 1862, alongside its beignets.

Chicory the coffee root and chicory the salad leaf are one species, Cichorium intybus, grown as different crops. Root chicory is bred for a large, fleshy root. The leaf chicories include red radicchio, puntarelle and Belgian endive, the pale, tight spears grown in the dark from chicory roots, while curly frisée and broad escarole are close cousins in the same genus. All share the bitterness the roasted root brings to the cup. Mind the names: in Britain the pale spears are sold as chicory and the curly leaf as endive.

Chicory went into coffee as a stretcher. In 1806 Britain blockaded the French coast and Napoleon answered with his Continental System, an embargo on British trade; imported coffee grew scarce in France, the French turned to roasted chicory root, and many kept the taste after the embargo ended. New Orleans, a French city and by 1840 the second largest coffee importer in the United States, kept the habit too. The story the city tells is the Civil War: from 1861 the Union blockade cut off the port and households stretched their coffee with chicory. It is true, but the French habit came first, so tell the blockade as tradition, not as the whole origin.

At Brennan's, the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake bakes chicory coffee into a bittersweet chocolate cake, where its roasty depth deepens the chocolate, with pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. It borrows the flavours of café brûlot, the city's flaming spiced coffee, so sell it as the coffee's flavours, not the flame. The house pours New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory, as the menu names it. How much chicory goes into it, and whether the cake uses the same blend, are questions for lineup.

Describe chicory as a roasted root, not a coffee, that gives our coffee a roasty, chocolatey depth and a smooth body; a guest who finds it bitter may prefer it with hot milk. Suggest the coffee cake to share at the start or as a sweet course with coffee. Questions about caffeine go to the service note and the kitchen; never guess at a decaffeinated option.

entries.title: Pecans
entries.summary: The pecan is a hickory nut native to the Mississippi valley and the South, rich, buttery and quick to toast. New Orleans cooks put it where French recipes put almonds: in pralines, pies, crusts for fish and butter sauces.
entries.guest: Pecans are native to Louisiana, and New Orleans cooks use them where French recipes use almonds, as in the pralines on our bread pudding; on the Pecan Gulf Fish they go into the pecan bordelaise.

paras: The pecan is the nut of a tall hickory tree, Carya illinoinensis, native to the Mississippi valley, Texas and northern Mexico. It grows wild along Louisiana's rivers and in orchards across the South. The nuts ripen in autumn: the green husk splits on the tree, and from about October into December the nuts fall or are shaken down.

Inside the thin shell sit two ridged halves, sweet and buttery, softer and richer than an almond, because a pecan is roughly seven parts in ten fat. That oil carries the flavour, and it is why pecans toast fast, burn fast and go stale fast. In the Creole kitchen the pecan took the almond's place, in the praline and in butters for fish.

Buy halves for garnish and cheaper pieces for crusts, crumbles and pralines. Good pecans are plump, evenly light gold to tan, with a clean, sweet smell. Shrivelled, dark or greasy nuts are old, and a sharp smell like paint or old crayons means the oil has gone rancid: no cooking fixes that. Keep shelled pecans airtight in the fridge for a few months or in the freezer for longer, away from onions and fish, whose smells they soak up, and taste one from every new case before it goes into a dish.

Toasting drives off moisture, warms the oil and browns the surface, so the nut turns crisp and its flavour deepens. Spread the pecans in one layer on a tray and toast them at 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirring halfway, until they smell nutty and the cut faces turn a shade darker, the colour of light toffee. Halves take longer than pieces. Tip them onto a cold tray at once: the oil holds heat, and nuts left on the hot tray keep cooking.

For a handful, use a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 5 minutes, tossing all the time and never walking away. The gap between toasted and burnt is a minute or less, and burnt pecans taste bitter and acrid; one scorched batch spoils a whole sauce, so throw it out and start again. Toast on the day, cool before chopping, and salt them while still warm if the dish wants it.

Pecans run from breakfast to dessert; pralines and the pecan bordelaise have their own entries. Pecan pie is a custard of eggs, sugar, syrup and butter poured over pecans in a pastry case and baked at about 175°C (347°F) for 50 to 60 minutes, until the centre barely wobbles.

For a pecan crust on fish, pulse raw pecans with breadcrumbs: they toast in the pan, while nuts toasted in advance scorch before the fish is done. Dip the fillet in flour, egg wash and the crumb, and cook it in butter and oil over medium heat: higher, and the nuts burn before the fish cooks through. A pecan butter sauce is a cousin of meunière, fish cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley: here toasted pecans are warmed in brown butter with lemon and parsley.

The name comes from an Algonquian word for a nut, carried into English through the French pacane. The orchard pecan began in Louisiana: in 1846 or 1847 Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, grafted wood from a tree with large, thin-shelled nuts onto other trees. His variety, later named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, and grafting made the pecan an orchard crop.

Pecans run through four dishes at Brennan's. On the Pecan Gulf Fish they go into the pecan bordelaise; confirm at lineup which bordelaise it is before pairing a wine. On the New Orleans Bread Pudding they arrive as pralines. The Baked Apple on the Traditional Breakfast bakes under an oat and pecan crumble, and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake carries pecans for crunch. Never call our pecans Louisiana-grown until the kitchen confirms the supplier.

Say pih-KAHN, the common Louisiana way; PEE-kan is heard across the South too, so never correct a guest. Pecans are a tree nut, and they travel through crusts, butters, crumbles, pralines and sauces where a guest may not expect them, so every nut question goes to the kitchen and the service note, never a verdict from you.

entries.title: Leidenheimer and New Orleans French bread
entries.summary: New Orleans French bread is a long loaf with a thin crust that shatters and a light, cottony crumb, softer than a Paris baguette. Leidenheimer, baking since 1896, makes the loaf most po-boys are built on.
entries.guest: The crisps on our Creole Caesar, in place of croutons, are made from Leidenheimer French bread: the city's po-boy loaf, from a family bakery founded in 1896.

paras: New Orleans French bread is the city's everyday loaf: long and slim, with a crust so thin it shatters into flakes at the first bite and a crumb so light it is almost cottony. Beside a Paris baguette it is softer, airier and less chewy, with a pale, crackly skin rather than a thick, hard crust. It is built to be split and filled: the crumb gives under fried shrimp or a ladle of gravy while the crust keeps its crackle.
That lightness has a price: the loaf stales fast. It is at its best on the day it is baked and dry by the next morning, which is why New Orleans kitchens have so many uses for yesterday's bread.

It is a lean dough of flour, water, yeast and salt, and some bakers add a little sugar or fat. A baker's working ratio for a lean French dough is about 65 parts water and 2 parts salt to 100 parts flour by weight, with 2 to 3 parts fresh yeast. Knead until smooth and stretchy, rise until doubled, about an hour, then shape long loaves and give them a second, generous rise, which builds the airy crumb. Slash the tops and bake with steam at about 230°C (446°F) for 18 to 25 minutes; the steam keeps the crust thin and lets the loaf open fully.

In a restaurant the loaf is bought, not baked. Keep it in its paper bag at room temperature, never in plastic, which softens the crust, and never in the fridge, which stales it faster. To revive a day-old loaf, pass it quickly under the tap and warm it at 180°C (356°F) for 4 to 6 minutes, then serve it at once. For bread crisps, slice thin on the bias, about 3 mm (1/8 inch), brush with butter or oil and bake at 160 to 175°C (320 to 347°F) for 8 to 12 minutes, until dry right through and golden at the edges.

The po-boy is the loaf's great use: a length of French bread split and filled with fried shrimp, fried oysters or roast beef in gravy. Ordered dressed, it carries shredded lettuce, sliced tomato, pickles and mayonnaise; plain means none of those. Drain fried fillings on a rack and dress the sandwich at the last moment, so the crumb stays crisp-edged rather than soggy.

Stale French bread is the base of two New Orleans classics with their own entries: bread pudding, the bread soaked in sweet custard and baked, and pain perdu, lost bread, slices dipped in egg and milk and fried. The light crumb drinks custard without turning to paste.

George Leidenheimer came from Deidesheim in Germany and opened his bakery on Dryades Street in 1896, baking the dense breads of home. His customers wanted the light, crisp loaf the city already loved, so he turned to French bread, and in 1904 the bakery moved to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes. The family has run it for four generations, by the bakery's own account.

Its bread is older than the po-boy, so never say Leidenheimer invented the sandwich. The story the city tells dates the name to the streetcar strike of 1929, when Bennie and Clovis Martin, former streetcar conductors with a restaurant by the French Market, fed striking poor boys free sandwiches. Historians note the brothers may have sold the sandwich before the strike, so tell it as the city's story.

At Brennan's the loaf becomes the Leidenheimer crisps on the Creole Caesar: thin toasted slices in place of croutons, with gem lettuce, a smoked oyster dressing and Grana Padano. The menu prints the name and nothing more, so how the crisps are cut and toasted, and whether with butter or oil, is a kitchen answer, never a guess.

Say LY-den-hy-mer. Naming the bread turns a garnish into a piece of New Orleans: the crisps come from the city's po-boy bread, from a bakery founded in 1896. A guest who asks whether the bakery is still family run can be told yes: the founder's family runs it, in its fourth generation. Wheat and gluten questions about the crisps or the dressing go to the kitchen and the service note.
