entries.title: Mirliton, satsuma and Creole cream cheese
entries.summary: Three foods of the New Orleans household larder: the mirliton, a pale green squash stuffed for the holidays; the satsuma, a seedless Plaquemines mandarin; and Creole cream cheese, a tangy cultured cheese eaten for breakfast. Each is rarely seen on restaurant menus.
entries.guest: Mirliton, satsumas and Creole cream cheese are New Orleans home cooking: a holiday squash, a local winter mandarin and a tangy breakfast cheese, more often met at a family table than on a menu.

paras: These three belong together because they belong to the house, not the restaurant. For generations they filled the household larder of New Orleans: a mirliton vine on the back fence, a bag of satsumas from down the river, a tub of Creole cream cheese from the corner creamery. Home cooks knew them by season; restaurant menus seldom printed them. Knowing them shows a cook what the city eats when it cooks for itself.

The mirliton is the chayote, a pale green, pear-shaped squash of the gourd family, creased at its broad end, with crisp, watery flesh, a mild taste between cucumber and courgette and one soft, flat seed. Many in the city say MEL-ih-tawn; MIR-lih-tahn is heard too. The vines fruit in autumn, which is why stuffed mirliton is a Thanksgiving and Christmas dish in New Orleans homes.

The satsuma is a seedless mandarin first grown in Japan, with a loose skin that peels in one go and sweet, juicy segments. It grows in Plaquemines Parish and across south Louisiana. Creole cream cheese is no foil-wrapped block: it is a soft, fresh farmer's cheese of skimmed milk, soured with a culture and set with a little rennet, nearer a thick yoghurt or fine ricotta, eaten with sugar and cream or fruit.

Mirlitons come in from autumn into early winter; choose firm, unblemished, pale green fruit, heavy for its size, with no soft spots or sprouting, and keep them loosely wrapped in the fridge for up to two weeks. Satsumas run roughly October to December. Choose fruit heavy for its size with snug skin; a puffy, light satsuma is past its best, and a green-tinged one may be ripe, because the skin colours late. Creole cream cheese comes fresh from a few small dairies: buy it close to its date and keep it cold.

Peel raw mirliton under running water or in gloves, because its sap leaves a sticky, tingling film on the hands. To stuff them, halve them lengthwise and simmer until a knife slides in, 30 to 45 minutes by size. Lift out the seed and scoop the flesh, leaving a shell about 6 mm (1/4 inch) thick. Chop the flesh and drain it well, then cook it down with onion, celery and green pepper sweated in butter until the water is gone. Fold in shrimp, crabmeat or diced ham with breadcrumbs to bind, fill the shells, top with crumbs and butter, and bake at 190°C (374°F) for 20 to 30 minutes until golden.

For Creole cream cheese, bring 3.8 litres (1 gallon) of pasteurised skimmed milk to room temperature, stir in 240 ml (1 cup) of cultured buttermilk and a few drops of rennet diluted in cool water, cover, and leave it at 21 to 24°C (70 to 75°F) for 12 to 24 hours, until it sets to a soft curd with clear whey at the edge. Ladle it gently into perforated moulds, drain it in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours, then keep it at 5°C (41°F) or below and use it within a week. Satsumas are best raw: segmented into salads, or juiced for vinaigrettes, glazes and a satsuma beurre blanc.

Creole cream cheese was once sold by many New Orleans dairies; as they closed through the twentieth century it nearly vanished. Around 2000 the New Orleans food writer and broadcaster Poppy Tooker, then a Slow Food leader, championed it for Slow Food's Ark of Taste, a catalogue of foods at risk of being lost, and small dairies, Mauthe's among them, began making it again. Mirlitons have had hard years too: heat and storms have killed many old backyard vines, and local growers now collect and share heirloom strains to keep them going.

None of the three is printed on our menus, so a question about them usually comes from a local with a memory or a curious cook. Meet it warmly: the mirliton is the holiday squash families stuff with shrimp and ham, the satsuma the winter mandarin from down the river, Creole cream cheese the old breakfast cheese eaten with sugar and cream. If a special uses one, learn it at lineup, and send any dairy or shellfish question about the dish to the kitchen.

steps.title: Shuck an oyster
steps.prompt: Put the stages of shucking an oyster for the half shell in order, from the cooler to the ice. One stage does not belong.
steps: Scrub the shells under cold running water, and throw out any that gape and will not close when tapped
Guard your holding hand with a folded towel or a cut-resistant glove, and hold the oyster cup side down, hinge towards you
Work the tip of the oyster knife into the hinge and twist until the shell pops
Wipe the blade clean of mud and grit before it goes back in
Slide the blade along the inside of the top shell to cut the muscle, and lift the top shell away
Keeping the cup level, run the blade under the oyster to free it from the bottom shell
With the oyster freed in its cup, check it by eye for grit and chipped shell, and smell it: an oyster that smells off is thrown away
Set it on crushed ice in its liquor, the salty juice in the shell, and send it at once
steps.distractor: Pour off the liquor and rinse the oyster under the tap so it looks clean
steps.why: Clean, live shells come first, and the hand is guarded before any knife goes in. The hinge is popped and the blade wiped so no grit falls in; the top muscle is cut, then the bottom, with the cup level. The liquor is part of the taste and is never poured away or rinsed off.
